newsitem.title: ITALY: ALPINE SKIING-KJUS AND MADER LOOK FOR SURPRISES.
newsitem.headline: ALPINE SKIING-KJUS AND MADER LOOK FOR SURPRISES.

text.p: Lasse Kjus and Guenther Mader, the two men who dominated the overall Alpine skiing World Cup last season, hope the opening race of the world championships on Monday will provide a surprise.

It may seem strange given their supremacy last year but if either man were to win the super-G on the fast and demanding Kandahar-Banchetta piste, it would indeed count as a surprise after a frustrating time for both.
A gold medal would be something for the Norwegian, whose season has been hit by misfortune. For Austrian veteran Mader, it would break the habit of a lifetime.
Neither all-rounder has a strong world championship record and neither has won a real race this season either.
Kjus, the Olympic and 1993 world combined champion, won four races in 1995-96 to run away with the World Cup.
Mader won twice and finished second.
Yet Kjus took only a silver medal in the combined at the 1996 world championships in Sierra Nevada and Mader joined him on the podium, behind as usual, with a third place.

Since then, Kjus's World Cup fortunes have declined dramatically due to illness and injury while the 32-year-old Mader, plagued by off-season back injuries, has been eclipsed in the Austrian team by younger men.

Mader, five times a bronze medallist in his career and world number two for the past two seasons, finished second in the opening super-G in Val d'Isere in December but has otherwise had little to celebrate.
The father of two -- his older son is nine years old -- is 11th in the World Cup while Kjus is 19th.
Both have had just one win this season -- in the combined which lacks the kudos of victory on the piste.
Sestriere might provide the breakthrough.
The Norwegian has nothing to lose, hardly any pressure and should be more relaxed than his rivals. He has also been training on the hill here since Friday.
Mader has the veteran's pressure of knowing these will be surely his last championships, tempered by the vast experience of a man completing 15 years of top-level skiing.
These will be the Innsbruck skier's sixth world championships and despite six medals including an Olympic downhill bronze in 1992 he has never won gold.
Others may see to it that he never does.
There have been just two men's World Cup super-G races this season and they have gone to Austrian Hans Knauss and France's Luc Alphand, who has also won three downhills.
Both will be front-runners again here as will Norwegian Kjetil-Andre Aamodt, the current World Cup leader.

Alphand, who lives just the other side of the border, can count on plenty of home support and his morale is sky-high after winning the first super-G of his career in Laax last week. He was not even trying too hard at the time.
The Frenchman was also a junior world champion in the Italian resort in 1983 and likes the hill.
There is no official timed training on the piste, which has not been used in its current shape before.
Although Alphand has never captured a major title outside the World Cup, he will also be the man to beat in downhill and has another good chance of gold in that.
Kristian Ghedina of Italy will be the home favourite after three downhill wins, while his compatriot Peter Runggaldier has a third place in super-G this season too.
But the super-G is always the most open of all the disciplines and last year's champion Atle Skaardal of Norway, another veteran, was again something of a surprise.
